title: Art & Culture
blurb: Painting, music, literature, cinema and architecture.

lessons.title: Great art movements
lessons.summary: From the Renaissance to modern art.

cards.title: The Renaissance
cards.text: In 15th–16th century Italy, artists revived ancient Greek and Roman ideas and studied anatomy and perspective. Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael are its giants.

cards.title: Linear perspective
cards.text: Renaissance painters used vanishing points: parallel lines converge to a point on the horizon, creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface.

cards.title: Baroque drama
cards.text: In the 1600s, Baroque art went for drama: strong light and dark (chiaroscuro), movement and emotion. Caravaggio, Rembrandt and Velázquez led the way.

cards.title: Impressionism
cards.text: In 1870s Paris, Monet, Renoir and Degas painted outdoors with quick brushstrokes, capturing light and moments rather than fine detail. The name started as an insult.

cards.title: Post-Impressionism
cards.text: Van Gogh, Cézanne and Gauguin pushed further: bold colours, expressive brushwork and simplified shapes. Van Gogh sold very few paintings in his lifetime.

cards.title: Cubism
cards.text: Picasso and Braque broke objects into geometric shapes and showed several viewpoints at once. *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon* (1907) shocked even their friends.

cards.title: Surrealism
cards.text: Surrealists like Dalí and Magritte painted dreams and the unconscious, inspired by Freud. Melting clocks and pipes that "are not a pipe" made viewers question reality.

cards.title: Abstract art
cards.text: Kandinsky and Mondrian made art that didn't depict anything recognisable: just colour, line and form. Later, Jackson Pollock dripped paint across canvases on the floor.

cards.title: Pop Art
cards.text: In the 1960s, Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein turned soup cans, celebrities and comics into art, blurring the line between art and advertising.

cards.title: Portuguese painters
cards.text: Portugal's art includes Nuno Gonçalves' 15th-century *Saint Vincent Panels*, Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso's modernism and Paula Rego's powerful storytelling.

quiz.q: Which movement captured light with quick outdoor brushstrokes?
quiz.explain: Monet's "Impression, Sunrise" gave it its name.

quiz.q: Who painted melting clocks?
Which technique creates depth with lines meeting at a point?

cards.title: Sound and pitch
cards.text: A note's pitch is its frequency: how many vibrations per second. The A above middle C is usually tuned to 440 Hz.

cards.title: The octave
cards.text: Doubling a frequency gives the same note an octave higher. Western music divides the octave into 12 semitones, the white and black keys of a piano.

cards.title: Scales
cards.text: A major scale follows a pattern of whole and half steps. Major tends to sound bright; minor tends to sound sadder.

cards.title: Chords
cards.text: A chord is notes played together. A major chord stacks a root, a major third and a fifth; C major is C, E and G.

cards.title: Four chords
cards.text: A huge number of pop songs use the same four chords, often I–V–vi–IV. In C major that's C, G, Am and F.

cards.title: Rhythm and tempo
cards.text: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds; tempo is the speed, measured in beats per minute. Most pop sits around 100–130 BPM.

cards.title: Instrument families
cards.text: Orchestras group instruments by how they make sound: strings, woodwind, brass and percussion.

cards.title: Classical eras
cards.text: Western classical music is often split into eras: Baroque (Bach), Classical (Mozart), Romantic (Beethoven to Tchaikovsky) and modern.

cards.title: Fado
cards.text: Fado, born in Lisbon in the early 1800s, is sung with Portuguese guitar and classical guitar and expresses *saudade*. Amália Rodrigues made it world famous. It's UNESCO-listed since 2011.

cards.title: Why music moves us
cards.text: Music triggers dopamine, especially just before an expected peak. Surprise and resolution, tension and release, are what give us chills.

quiz.q: What is the frequency of concert A?
Which notes make a C major chord?

cards.title: The oldest stories
cards.text: The *Epic of Gilgamesh*, from ancient Mesopotamia, is one of the oldest surviving stories, more than 4,000 years old. It's about friendship, loss and the search for immortality.

cards.title: Homer
cards.text: The *Iliad* tells of the Trojan War; the *Odyssey* follows Odysseus' 10-year journey home. Both were probably composed orally before being written down.

cards.title: The hero's journey
cards.text: Joseph Campbell found a common pattern in myths: a hero leaves home, faces trials, wins a prize and returns changed. *Star Wars* used it on purpose.

cards.title: Shakespeare

items.l: words first recorded in his work

cards.text: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote around 39 plays and 154 sonnets, and gave English hundreds of words and phrases, like "break the ice".

cards.title: Os Lusíadas
cards.text: Luís de Camões' epic poem (1572) celebrates Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and Portuguese history. 10 June, Portugal's national day, marks Camões' death.

cards.title: The novel
cards.text: The novel grew in the 17th–18th centuries. *Don Quixote* (1605) is often called the first modern novel; the 19th century brought Austen, Dickens, Tolstoy and Eça de Queirós.

cards.title: Saramago
cards.text: José Saramago won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998, the first writer in Portuguese to do so. His novels, like *Blindness*, use long sentences with little punctuation.

cards.title: Genres
cards.text: Literature has families: tragedy and comedy from the Greeks, plus poetry, novels, science fiction, crime, fantasy and more. Many books mix them.

cards.title: Show, don't tell

items.r: "She checked her phone for the third time in a minute"

cards.text: Writers make readers feel by showing actions and details rather than stating emotions directly.

cards.title: Why fiction matters
cards.text: Studies suggest reading fiction may improve our ability to understand others' feelings, by practising seeing through someone else's eyes.

quiz.q: Which Portuguese writer won the Nobel Prize in 1998?
What does Os Lusíadas celebrate?
options: Vasco da Gama's voyage and Portuguese history

lessons.title: Cinema
lessons.summary: How moving pictures work and changed the world.

cards.title: The illusion of motion
cards.text: Film is a series of still images shown quickly, usually 24 frames per second. The brain blends them into smooth motion.

cards.title: The birth of cinema
cards.text: In 1895 the Lumière brothers showed short films to a paying audience in Paris. Georges Méliès soon invented special effects with *A Trip to the Moon* (1902).

cards.title: Silent era to sound
cards.text: *The Jazz Singer* (1927) brought synchronised dialogue. Many silent stars, like Charlie Chaplin, struggled or resisted at first.

cards.title: The language of shots
cards.text: Shot size tells you what to feel. Wide shots show place and scale; close-ups show emotion; over-the-shoulder shots put you in a conversation.

cards.title: Editing
cards.text: Editing is invisible storytelling. The Kuleshov effect showed that the same neutral face seems hungry, sad or loving depending on the shot that follows it.

cards.title: Three-act structure
cards.text: Most films follow three acts: set-up, confrontation and resolution, with turning points between them.

cards.title: Sound and music
cards.text: Music guides emotion. Two notes from *Jaws* or the opening of *Star Wars* can make you feel something before you see anything.

cards.title: Animation
cards.text: Animation creates motion frame by frame, by hand, stop-motion or computer. *Toy Story* (1995) was the first fully computer-animated feature film.

cards.title: Portuguese cinema
cards.text: Manoel de Oliveira directed films for over 80 years, until he was over 100. Directors like João César Monteiro and Pedro Costa won prizes abroad.

cards.title: Watch like a filmmaker
cards.text: Next time you watch a film, notice: how long the shots last, when the music starts, and where the camera is when a character makes a big decision.

quiz.q: How many frames per second does film usually use?
What did the Kuleshov effect show?
options: Editing changes how we read a face

lessons.title: Architecture and design
lessons.summary: Buildings, styles and the art of everyday things.

cards.title: Classical orders
cards.text: Greek and Roman architecture used column styles called orders: Doric (simple), Ionic (scrolls) and Corinthian (leaves).

cards.title: The arch
cards.text: Romans perfected the arch, which turns a load into sideways forces carried down to the ground. With concrete, they built the Pantheon dome, still unreinforced and standing.

cards.title: Gothic
cards.text: Gothic cathedrals (12th–16th centuries) used pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to build higher walls full of stained glass.

cards.title: Manueline style
cards.text: Portugal's own late-Gothic style, named after King Manuel I, decorates buildings with ropes, shells, armillary spheres and sea motifs. See the Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower.

cards.title: Azulejos
cards.text: Portugal's painted tiles, inspired by Moorish designs, cover churches, stations and houses. The blue-and-white style became popular in the 17th–18th centuries.

cards.title: Pombaline Baixa
cards.text: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt on a grid with the "gaiola pombalina", a wooden frame designed to flex in earthquakes: one of the first anti-seismic designs.

cards.title: Form follows function
cards.text: Modernist architects argued buildings should be shaped by what they do, not decoration. Le Corbusier called a house "a machine for living in".

cards.title: Siza and Souto de Moura

events.l: Souto de Moura wins the Pritzker

cards.text: Portuguese architects Álvaro Siza (1992) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (2011) both won the Pritzker Prize, architecture's top honour.

cards.title: Good design
cards.text: Designer Dieter Rams proposed principles of good design, including: useful, understandable, honest, long-lasting and "as little design as possible".

cards.title: Golden ratio myths

items.w: "The Parthenon is built on the golden ratio"
items.r: An appealing story without solid evidence

cards.text: The golden ratio (about 1.618) appears in maths and some art, but many claims, like the Parthenon or the Mona Lisa being built on it, are unproven.

quiz.q: Which style is Portugal's own, seen in the Jerónimos Monastery?
Which Portuguese architects won the Pritzker Prize?
quiz.explain: Álvaro Siza (1992) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (2011).

cards.title: Leonardo da Vinci
cards.text: Leonardo (1452–1519) was painter, engineer, anatomist and inventor. Only around 15–20 paintings are firmly attributed to him, but his notebooks fill thousands of pages.

cards.title: The Mona Lisa
cards.text: Painted from about 1503, the Mona Lisa's fame comes from its soft blending (sfumato), mysterious smile and a 1911 theft that made headlines worldwide.

cards.title: Sfumato
cards.text: Leonardo blended colours and tones so softly that edges seem to dissolve, like smoke. It gives faces life and mystery.

cards.title: The Last Supper
cards.text: Leonardo's mural in Milan captures the moment Jesus says one apostle will betray him. He experimented with paint on dry plaster, so it began flaking within decades.

cards.title: Michelangelo
cards.text: Michelangelo (1475–1564) saw himself as a sculptor first. He carved David from a single block of marble in his twenties.

cards.title: The Sistine ceiling
cards.text: Michelangelo painted over 300 figures on the Sistine Chapel ceiling in about four years, standing on scaffolding and craning his neck, not lying on his back.

cards.title: Raphael
cards.text: Raphael (1483–1520) was famous for harmony and grace. His *School of Athens* gathers ancient philosophers, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre.

cards.title: Patrons
cards.text: Renaissance art was paid for by wealthy patrons: the Medici in Florence, popes in Rome and guilds. Contracts often specified colours and figures.

cards.title: Northern Renaissance
cards.text: North of the Alps, artists like Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer perfected oil paint and astonishing detail.

cards.title: Rivalries
cards.text: Leonardo and Michelangelo were rivals, once painting opposite walls of the same hall in Florence. Neither finished.

quiz.q: What is sfumato?
What did Michelangelo consider himself first?
Who painted the School of Athens?
quiz.explain: Plato and Aristotle at the centre.

cards.title: Carving and modelling
cards.text: Sculptors either carve away material, like stone or wood, or build it up by modelling clay or wax, often later cast in bronze.

cards.title: Lost-wax casting
cards.text: To cast bronze, a wax model is covered in clay, heated so the wax melts out, and molten bronze is poured into the space.

cards.title: Ancient Greece
cards.text: Greek sculptors moved from stiff figures to natural poses. Contrapposto, weight on one leg, made statues look alive.

cards.title: Painted statues
cards.text: Ancient statues weren't pure white: they were brightly painted. The paint wore off over centuries; traces are found with UV light.

cards.title: Bernini
cards.text: Gian Lorenzo Bernini made marble seem soft as flesh. In *The Rape of Proserpina*, Pluto's fingers press into her thigh.

cards.title: Rodin
cards.text: Auguste Rodin's *The Thinker* (1880) began as part of a huge door, *The Gates of Hell*, representing Dante.

cards.title: Modern sculpture
cards.text: In the 20th century, sculptors like Brâncuși, Giacometti and Henry Moore simplified forms, used holes and voids, and explored new materials.

cards.title: Public art
cards.text: Sculpture shapes cities: monuments, fountains and installations. Lisbon's Padrão dos Descobrimentos (1960) celebrates navigators.

cards.title: Portuguese sculptors
cards.text: Machado de Castro made Lisbon's equestrian statue of King José I (1775). Contemporary artist Joana Vasconcelos creates monumental works from everyday objects.

cards.title: Land art
cards.text: Some artists sculpt the landscape itself: Robert Smithson's *Spiral Jetty* (1970) is a coil of rock 460 m long in Utah's Great Salt Lake.

quiz.q: How do sculptors cast bronze?
quiz.explain: Wax melted out, bronze poured in.

quiz.q: What colour were ancient Greek statues originally?

cards.title: The camera obscura
cards.text: For centuries artists used the camera obscura, a dark room or box with a small hole that projects an upside-down image. Capturing that image permanently came later.

cards.title: The first photographs
cards.text: The oldest surviving photograph from a camera, by Nicéphore Niépce, dates from around 1826–27 and needed hours of exposure. Daguerre's process followed in 1839.

cards.title: Exposure triangle
cards.text: Three settings control exposure: aperture (how wide the lens opens), shutter speed (how long) and ISO (how sensitive the sensor is).

cards.title: Rule of thirds

items.r: Place it on a third line

cards.text: Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid and place the subject on a line or intersection. It usually feels more dynamic than dead centre.

cards.title: Golden hour
cards.text: The hour after sunrise and before sunset gives soft, warm, low light with long shadows, loved by photographers.

cards.title: Photojournalism
cards.text: Photographs have shaped history: Capa's war images, the "Napalm Girl" in Vietnam, the "Earthrise" from Apollo 8. A single image can change public opinion.

cards.title: Portrait tips
cards.text: Focus on the eyes, use soft side light, shoot at eye level and give people something to do. Candid moments often beat posed ones.

cards.title: Smartphone revolution
cards.text: Phone cameras use computational photography, combining many frames instantly to reduce noise and extend dynamic range. Billions of photos are taken every day.

cards.title: Photography as art
cards.text: For decades critics debated whether photography was art. Today photographers like Cartier-Bresson and Annie Leibovitz are in major museums.

cards.title: Truth and manipulation
cards.text: Photos were edited long before Photoshop, like Stalin removing purged officials. Today AI makes convincing fakes easy, so provenance matters.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the exposure triangle?
When is "golden hour"?
options: Just after sunrise and before sunset

cards.title: Portuguese guitar
cards.text: The Portuguese guitar has 12 strings in six pairs and a pear-shaped body, giving fado its shimmering sound. Carlos Paredes made it famous as a solo instrument.

cards.title: Coimbra fado
cards.text: Coimbra fado is sung by men, traditionally students in black capes, often as serenades. It's more lyrical and academic than Lisbon fado.

cards.title: Azulejo museum
cards.text: Lisbon's National Azulejo Museum, in the Madre de Deus convent, shows five centuries of tiles, including a 23-metre panorama of Lisbon before the 1755 earthquake.

cards.title: Calçada portuguesa
cards.text: Portugal's black and white stone pavements are laid by hand by calceteiros. The waves of Rossio square inspired Copacabana's promenade in Rio.

cards.title: Filigree
cards.text: Portuguese filigree, especially from Gondomar and Póvoa de Lanhoso, twists fine gold and silver threads into delicate jewellery, like the heart of Viana.

cards.title: Festas populares
cards.text: In June, cities celebrate saints: Santo António in Lisbon with grilled sardines and basil pots, São João in Porto with plastic hammers and leeks.

cards.title: Barcelos rooster
cards.text: The Barcelos rooster legend tells of a pilgrim wrongly accused of theft; a roasted rooster crowed to prove his innocence. It became a national symbol.

cards.title: Literature beyond Camões
cards.text: Fernando Pessoa, Eça de Queirós, Sophia de Mello Breyner and José Saramago are pillars of Portuguese literature.

cards.title: Cante alentejano
cards.text: Alentejo's polyphonic choral singing, without instruments, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014. Groups of men or women sing slow, deep songs about the land.

cards.title: The language
cards.text: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people across four continents, the most spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere.

quiz.q: How many strings does the Portuguese guitar have?
Which city celebrates São João with plastic hammers?

cards.title: What makes poetry
cards.text: Poetry uses rhythm, sound, imagery and line breaks to compress meaning and feeling. It's meant to be heard as much as read.

cards.title: Metre
cards.text: Metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Shakespeare's iambic pentameter has five da-DUM beats: "shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY".

cards.title: The sonnet
cards.text: A sonnet has 14 lines. Petrarch popularised it in Italy; Shakespeare wrote 154; Camões wrote hundreds of sonnets in Portuguese.

cards.title: Haiku
cards.text: The Japanese haiku traditionally has 5–7–5 sound units and captures a moment in nature. Bashō's frog jumping into an old pond is the most famous.

cards.title: Metaphor and simile
cards.text: A simile compares using "like" or "as"; a metaphor says one thing *is* another. "Life is a journey" shapes how we think about life.

cards.title: Free verse
cards.text: Since the late 1800s, many poets abandoned regular rhyme and metre. Walt Whitman's long lines and Pessoa's Álvaro de Campos broke the old rules.

cards.title: Pessoa's Mensagem
cards.text: Fernando Pessoa's *Mensagem* (1934), the only book in Portuguese he published in his lifetime, reimagines Portuguese history as myth. "O mar salgado, quanto do teu sal / São lágrimas de Portugal!"

cards.title: Florbela Espanca
cards.text: Florbela Espanca (1894–1930) wrote passionate, intense sonnets about love, longing and identity, and is one of Portugal's most beloved poets.

cards.title: Spoken word
cards.text: From ancient bards to rap and slam poetry, poetry has always been performed. Rap uses rhyme, rhythm and wordplay as intensely as any sonnet.

cards.title: Reading a poem
cards.text: Read it aloud twice. Notice what surprises you, which images stay with you, where the lines break and what changes by the end.

quiz.q: How many lines does a sonnet have?
quiz.explain: Petrarch and Shakespeare used different structures.

quiz.q: What is a metaphor?
Which Pessoa book was published in his lifetime?

cards.title: Greek theatre
cards.text: Theatre as we know it began in Athens in the 5th century BCE, at festivals for the god Dionysus. Huge open-air theatres seated thousands.

cards.title: Tragedy and comedy
cards.text: Greek tragedy showed noble heroes destroyed by a fatal flaw; comedy mocked politicians and society. The two masks still symbolise theatre.

cards.title: Gil Vicente
cards.text: Gil Vicente (c. 1465–1536) is the father of Portuguese theatre. His *Auto da Barca do Inferno* satirises sinners of all classes waiting to board the boats to heaven or hell.

cards.title: Shakespeare's Globe
cards.text: Shakespeare's plays were performed at the Globe, an open-air theatre in London where groundlings stood for a penny. All roles were played by men.

cards.title: Commedia dell'arte
cards.text: Italian improvised comedy used stock characters with masks, like Harlequin and Pantalone. It influenced Molière and modern sitcoms.

cards.title: Opera
cards.text: Opera began in Italy around 1600, combining drama, music and spectacle. Lisbon's Teatro Nacional de São Carlos opened in 1793.

cards.title: Realism
cards.text: In the 1800s, Ibsen and Chekhov brought ordinary homes and psychological depth to the stage, instead of kings and gods.

cards.title: Breaking the fourth wall
cards.text: The "fourth wall" is the invisible wall between actors and audience. Brecht broke it on purpose, so viewers would think critically rather than get lost in illusion.

cards.title: Musicals
cards.text: Musicals blend songs, dialogue and dance. Broadway and London's West End host long-running shows seen by millions.

cards.title: Theatre of the Absurd
cards.text: After the Second World War, playwrights like Beckett wrote plays where little happens. In *Waiting for Godot*, two men wait for someone who never arrives.

quiz.q: Who is the father of Portuguese theatre?
In which city did theatre as we know it begin?

cards.title: Serif and sans serif
cards.text: Serifs are small strokes at the end of letters; sans-serif fonts have none. Serifs feel traditional; sans serif feels modern and clean.

cards.title: Gutenberg
cards.text: Around 1450, Gutenberg's movable-type press made books far cheaper, spreading literacy, science and new ideas across Europe.

cards.title: Hierarchy
cards.text: Good design guides the eye: the most important thing is biggest or boldest, then the next. Without hierarchy, everything shouts at once.

cards.title: White space
cards.text: Empty space isn't wasted. It gives elements room to breathe and makes designs feel calm and premium.

cards.title: The grid
cards.text: Designers use invisible grids to align elements consistently. Magazines, websites and posters all rely on them.

cards.title: Logos
cards.text: A great logo is simple, memorable and works at any size, even in one colour. The best are recognisable from their shape alone.

cards.title: Bauhaus
cards.text: The Bauhaus school (1919–1933) in Germany merged art, craft and industry. "Form follows function" and clean geometric design shaped modern design.

cards.title: Swiss style
cards.text: Mid-century Swiss designers used grids, sans-serif type and objective layouts. Helvetica (1957) came from this movement.

cards.title: Readability
cards.text: For body text, around 50–75 characters per line, decent size and strong contrast make reading comfortable.

cards.title: Design is problem-solving
cards.text: Design isn't decoration. It solves problems: a clear road sign, an easy form, a usable app. Test with real people.

quiz.q: What are serifs?
options: Small strokes at the end of letters

quiz.q: When did the Bauhaus close?

lessons.title: Colour
lessons.summary: How it works and how it makes us feel.

cards.title: The colour wheel
cards.text: Painters' primary colours (red, yellow, blue) mix into secondaries (orange, green, purple). Colours opposite each other are complementary.

cards.title: Light vs paint
cards.text: Light mixes additively: red, green and blue make white, as on screens. Paint mixes subtractively: cyan, magenta and yellow make dark, as in printers.

cards.title: Hue, saturation, value
cards.text: Hue is the colour family, saturation is its intensity and value is its lightness. Changing value often matters more than changing hue.

cards.title: Colour harmonies
cards.text: Designers combine colours using simple rules: complementary for contrast, analogous (neighbours) for calm, triadic for balance.

cards.title: Warm and cool
cards.text: Reds, oranges and yellows feel warm and seem to come forward; blues and greens feel cool and recede.

cards.title: Colour and culture

items.b: weddings in the West, mourning in parts of Asia

cards.text: Colour meanings vary: white is for weddings in much of the West but for mourning in parts of Asia. Red means luck in China and danger on road signs.

cards.title: Expensive blue
cards.text: Ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan, was once worth more than gold. Painters often reserved it for the Virgin Mary's robes.

cards.title: Colour blindness
cards.text: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have colour vision deficiency, usually difficulty telling red and green apart. Good design never relies on colour alone.

cards.title: Simultaneous contrast
cards.text: The same grey looks lighter on black and darker on white. Colours change depending on their neighbours.

cards.title: Klein blue
cards.text: In 1960, artist Yves Klein patented his own intense ultramarine, International Klein Blue, and painted monochrome canvases with it.

quiz.q: Mixing red, green and blue light makes…
Roughly how many men have colour vision deficiency?

cards.title: Blues roots
cards.text: The blues grew from African American communities in the US South around 1900, from work songs and spirituals. Its 12-bar form underlies rock and roll.

cards.title: Jazz
cards.text: Jazz, born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, emphasises improvisation and swing. Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Miles Davis shaped it.

cards.title: Rock and roll
cards.text: In the 1950s, Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Elvis Presley fused blues, gospel and country. Teenagers had their own music for the first time.

cards.title: The Beatles
cards.text: The Beatles transformed pop between 1962 and 1970, from simple love songs to studio experiments. They remain the best-selling act in history.

cards.title: Hip hop
cards.text: Hip hop began in the Bronx in the 1970s with DJs looping breakbeats at block parties. It's now one of the world's most listened-to genres.

cards.title: Electronic music
cards.text: Synthesisers and drum machines led to disco, house, techno and EDM. Detroit and Chicago shaped techno and house in the 1980s.

cards.title: Music videos
cards.text: MTV launched in 1981 with "Video Killed the Radio Star". Michael Jackson's *Thriller* (1982) became the best-selling album ever.

cards.title: Portuguese pop
cards.text: Portugal's music ranges from fado to Zeca Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena", signal for the 1974 revolution, to Salvador Sobral's 2017 Eurovision win.

cards.title: Streaming
cards.text: Streaming now accounts for most recorded music revenue. Artists earn fractions of a cent per stream, so touring matters more than ever.

cards.title: Why songs get stuck
cards.text: Earworms tend to have simple, repetitive melodies with an unexpected twist. Chewing gum or doing a puzzle can help get rid of them.

quiz.q: Which song signalled Portugal's 1974 revolution?
Where did hip hop begin?

cards.title: Why we dance
cards.text: Every known culture dances: for celebration, worship, courtship and storytelling. Dancing releases endorphins and bonds groups.

cards.title: Ballet
cards.text: Ballet began in Italian and French courts in the 15th–17th centuries. Louis XIV, a keen dancer, founded the first dance academy in 1661. French terms are still used worldwide.

cards.title: Swan Lake
cards.text: Tchaikovsky's *Swan Lake* (1877) was a flop at first. Revived in 1895, it became the most performed ballet in the world.

cards.title: Modern dance
cards.text: Isadora Duncan danced barefoot and freely; Martha Graham built a technique from breathing and contraction. Modern dance rebelled against ballet's rules.

cards.title: The tango
cards.text: Tango was born in the working-class districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s, mixing European, African and local influences.

cards.title: Portuguese folk dances
cards.text: Portugal's folk dances include the vira of the Minho, the corridinho of the Algarve and the pauliteiros' stick dances of Miranda do Douro.

cards.title: Flamenco
cards.text: Flamenco from Andalusia combines singing, guitar, dance and handclaps, with Romani, Moorish and Andalusian roots. UNESCO-listed in 2010.

cards.title: Street dance
cards.text: Breaking, locking, popping and krumping grew from streets and clubs. Breaking even debuted at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

cards.title: Kizomba
cards.text: Kizomba, a close partner dance from Angola, spread through Lisbon's clubs to become popular across Europe.

cards.title: Dance and the brain
cards.text: Dancing combines rhythm, memory, balance and social connection. Studies link it to better balance and wellbeing in older adults.

quiz.q: Which dance is from the Minho region?
Which dance style appeared at the Paris 2024 Olympics?

cards.title: Why myths matter
cards.text: Myths explain the world, teach values and give communities shared identity. Their characters and plots still shape films, books and everyday words.

cards.title: Greek gods
cards.text: The Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus, led by Zeus. They were powerful but very human: jealous, vain and often quarrelling.

cards.title: Words from myths
cards.text: Many words come from myths: "panic" from the god Pan, "echo" from a nymph, "narcissist" from Narcissus, "Achilles' heel" from Achilles.

cards.title: Roman versions
cards.text: Romans adopted Greek gods under new names. Our planets carry the Roman names.

cards.title: Norse myths
cards.text: Norse mythology features Odin, Thor and Loki, the world tree Yggdrasil and Ragnarök, the end of the world. Our weekdays Wednesday to Friday are named after Norse gods.

cards.title: Egyptian myths
cards.text: Osiris was killed by his brother Set and brought back by Isis, becoming lord of the afterlife. The dead's hearts were weighed against a feather.

cards.title: Creation stories
cards.text: Almost every culture has a creation story: from chaos, from an egg, from the body of a giant, or from a word. Comparing them reveals shared human questions.

cards.title: The flood
cards.text: Flood stories appear in Mesopotamia (Gilgamesh), the Bible (Noah), Greece (Deucalion) and India (Manu). Some may echo real ancient floods.

cards.title: Portuguese legends
cards.text: Portugal has legends of mouras encantadas, enchanted Moorish maidens guarding treasures, and King Sebastião, expected to return on a foggy morning.

cards.title: Myths today
cards.text: Superheroes, Star Wars and fantasy sagas borrow from myth: heroes, mentors, quests and monsters. Thor is now a Marvel character.

quiz.q: Which word comes from the god Pan?
Thursday is named after which god?
Who did the Portuguese expect to return on a foggy morning?

cards.title: Clothes as language
cards.text: Clothes signal identity, status, belonging and mood. Uniforms, subcultures and dress codes all communicate without words.

cards.title: Silk Road
cards.text: Silk, made in China for thousands of years, was so valuable that trade routes across Asia were named after it. Its production was a closely guarded secret.

cards.title: Industrial revolution
cards.text: Spinning and weaving machines in 18th-century Britain made cloth cheap, transforming fashion and work, and creating harsh factory conditions.

cards.title: Haute couture
cards.text: In the 1850s Charles Frederick Worth in Paris became the first designer to sign his work. Haute couture means handmade, made-to-measure fashion.

cards.title: Chanel
cards.text: Coco Chanel freed women from corsets with comfortable jersey, the little black dress (1926) and trousers. Comfort became chic.

cards.title: Denim
cards.text: Jeans began as workwear: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted denim trousers in 1873. Later, film stars made them a symbol of youth.

cards.title: Fast fashion
cards.text: Fast fashion copies runway trends in weeks at low prices. The industry produces large shares of global textile waste and emissions.

cards.title: Portugal's textile industry

items: Textiles in the Vale do Ave
Shoes in Felgueiras and São João da Madeira

cards.text: Northern Portugal, around Guimarães, Braga and Porto, has a strong textile and shoe industry, producing for major global brands. Portuguese shoes are among Europe's most exported.

cards.title: Sustainable fashion
cards.text: Buying fewer, better clothes, repairing, swapping and second-hand shopping reduce fashion's footprint. The most sustainable garment is the one you already own.

cards.title: Reading a label
cards.text: Check fibre content and care instructions. Natural fibres like wool and linen breathe; synthetics shed microplastics when washed.

quiz.q: Who popularised the little black dress?
Why were trade routes called the Silk Road?
options: Silk was a precious traded good

cards.title: Cooking made us human?
cards.text: Some anthropologists argue cooking helped humans evolve big brains by making food easier to digest and release more energy.

cards.title: The Columbian exchange
cards.text: After 1492, crops crossed oceans: tomatoes, potatoes, chillies and maize came to Europe; wheat, sugar and coffee spread to the Americas.

cards.title: Portuguese spice trade
cards.text: Portuguese navigators spread chillies to India, tempura to Japan and pão de ló to Japan as castella. Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese "vinha d'alhos".

cards.title: Bacalhau

steps: Cod caught in the North Atlantic

cards.text: Portugal eats about 20% of the world's cod, though cod doesn't swim in Portuguese waters. Salting allowed it to keep on long voyages. Legend says there are 365 recipes, or 1,001.

cards.title: Pastel de nata
cards.text: Monks at the Jerónimos Monastery made custard tarts using leftover egg yolks, since whites were used to starch clothes. After 1834, the recipe went to a nearby bakery in Belém.

cards.title: The Mediterranean diet
cards.text: UNESCO recognised the Mediterranean diet, including Portugal, in 2013. Olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish and shared meals are its pillars.

cards.title: Umami
cards.text: Umami, the fifth taste, was identified in 1908 by Kikunae Ikeda in Japanese dashi broth. It's the savoury taste of tomatoes, cheese and broths.

cards.title: Fermentation
cards.text: Many cuisines rely on fermentation: cheese, bread, wine, kimchi, soy sauce. Microbes transform flavour and preserve food.

cards.title: Wine regions
cards.text: Portugal has over 250 native grape varieties. The Douro, demarcated in 1756, produces port wine, fortified with grape spirit to stop fermentation.

cards.title: The Maillard reaction
cards.text: Browning toast, seared steak and roasted coffee taste rich because of the Maillard reaction between sugars and proteins at high heat.

quiz.q: Which Indian dish takes its name from Portuguese "vinha d'alhos"?
Who first identified umami?

cards.title: Ancient games
cards.text: Board games are ancient: Senet in Egypt, the Royal Game of Ur in Mesopotamia and Go in China, played for over 2,500 years.

cards.title: Chess
cards.text: Chess emerged in India around the 6th century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia and the Arab world and reached Europe around 1000. The powerful queen appeared in the 1400s.

cards.title: Video games
cards.text: From *Pong* (1972) to open-world adventures, video games became the biggest entertainment industry, larger than film and music combined.

cards.title: Are games art?
cards.text: Games combine visuals, music, writing and interaction. Museums like MoMA now collect them, though critics once said they couldn't be art.

cards.title: Game design
cards.text: Good games balance challenge and skill, give clear goals and satisfying feedback: the same ingredients as "flow" in psychology.

cards.title: Comics
cards.text: Comics tell stories in sequences of images. Modern comic strips grew in newspapers in the 1890s; superhero comic books boomed from 1938.

cards.title: Manga
cards.text: Japanese manga is read from right to left and covers every genre. Osamu Tezuka, creator of *Astro Boy*, shaped its style.

cards.title: Graphic novels
cards.text: Long-form comics like *Maus*, which won a Pulitzer Prize in 1992, showed comics can tackle serious history and memoir.

cards.title: Portuguese comics
cards.text: The Amadora International Comics Festival, since 1990, is one of Portugal's biggest cultural events. Portuguese artists draw for major international publishers.

cards.title: Board game renaissance
cards.text: Modern board games like *Catan* (1995) and cooperative games sparked a boom in tabletop gaming, with thousands of new titles each year.

quiz.q: Where did chess originate?
Which graphic novel won a Pulitzer Prize?

cards.title: The Starry Night
cards.text: Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* in 1889 from memory, while in an asylum in Saint-Rémy. Its swirling sky is among the most recognised images in art.

cards.title: Las Meninas
cards.text: Velázquez's *Las Meninas* (1656) shows the painter himself at work, with the royal couple reflected in a mirror. Who is looking at whom?

cards.title: Guernica
cards.text: Picasso's *Guernica* (1937) responded to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. Its broken figures became a universal anti-war symbol.

cards.title: The Scream
cards.text: Edvard Munch's *The Scream* (1893) expresses anxiety: a figure under a blood-red sky. Munch made several versions in paint and print.

cards.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
cards.text: Vermeer's painting (c. 1665) isn't a portrait but a "tronie", a study of a face. Vermeer made only about 35 known paintings.

cards.title: The Great Wave
cards.text: Hokusai's *The Great Wave off Kanagawa* (c. 1831) is a woodblock print, made in thousands of copies. It inspired European artists like Monet and Van Gogh.

cards.title: Temptations of St Anthony
cards.text: Hieronymus Bosch's *The Temptations of St Anthony* is in Lisbon's National Museum of Ancient Art, full of fantastical creatures.

cards.title: The Gulbenkian
cards.text: Lisbon's Calouste Gulbenkian Museum holds a collector's treasures, from Egyptian art to Lalique jewellery. Gulbenkian, an oil magnate, spent his last years in Lisbon.

cards.title: Most visited museums
cards.text: The Louvre welcomes around 9 million visitors a year, more than any other art museum. The Mona Lisa sits behind bulletproof glass.

cards.title: Visiting a big museum
cards.text: Pick five works to see properly instead of rushing past hundreds. Arrive early, sit with one painting and read the label after looking.

quiz.q: What did Picasso's Guernica respond to?
options: The bombing of a Basque town

quiz.q: Where is Bosch's Temptations of St Anthony?
options: National Museum of Ancient Art, Lisbon
